_readme: THE ALERT DEFINITIONS. Config-as-code: this file plus census.py IS the
alert surface, and apply.py reconciles a ClickStack to it. Nothing here
names a destination URL, a token, a laptop, or any interactive tool — the
delivery URL is read at apply time from the Secrets Manager slot named in
`webhook.url_slot` (house doctrine: slot and length only, never a value).
The SHAPES are here; the POPULATION is census.py's, derived from
apps/*/events.py. `transition` is instantiated once per derived pair,
Placeholders are Python str.format fields, filled from the census row —
except `{namespace}` in the webhook block below, which apply.py fills from
DJB_DEPLOY_NAMESPACE and REFUSES to guess: the bundle name and the secret
slot are this deployment's own coordinates and no file in this repository

webhook.name: {namespace}-alerts
webhook.url_slot: {namespace}/<env>/env  key SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL  (ADR deploy-3a: one JSON secret per environment)
_service_note: `generic`, not `slack`, and that is deliberate and portable. ClickStack
refuses a `slack` webhook whose host does not end in slack.com
(isValidSlackUrl), which would make the laptop definition and the
staging definition two different definitions. A `generic` webhook posts
the rendered body verbatim, and the body below is `{"text": ...}` —
exactly what a Slack incoming webhook accepts and exactly what the dummy
receiver logs. ONE definition, two destinations, the slot the only
_body_note: SINGLE QUOTES inside the handlebars subexpression, and that is load-bearing.
ClickStack compiles this string with handlebars BEFORE it is ever JSON, so a
\" that keeps the JSON valid reaches the parser as backslash-quote and dies
with 'Parse error ... got INVALID' — the notification is then dropped with
one line in /var/log/app.log inside the sink container and NOTHING arrives
at the destination. That failure mode is exactly what the dummy receiver
takes 'ALERT' in single quotes, and a single quote is legal inside a JSON
string, so both parsers are happy.
_one_webhook_note: ONE WEBHOOK, AND CLICKSTACK ENFORCES THAT. A second webhook pointing at
the same URL is refused with 400 `Webhook already exists` — it is unique
by URL, not by name — so the recovery alert cannot be given its own
webhook just to make its OPEN say RECOVERED.
So the ALERT branch below renders `{{body}}` — the ALERT'S OWN MESSAGE —
and nothing else. Each alert therefore owns its own opening sentence,
emoji and verb, which is what lets `<x> degraded` open with a rotating
light and `<x> recovered` open with a white check mark through one
webhook and one destination. The OK branch is the same sentence for every
alert, because it means the same thing for every alert: the query window
stopped matching. It is deliberately NOT a verdict about the circuit.
webhook.body: {"text": "{{#if (eq state 'ALERT')}}{{body}}{{else}}:mag: window quiet — {{title}} — the query window stopped matching, which is NOT a verdict about the circuit{{/if}}\n{{link}}\nhdx_state={{state}} hdx_event_id={{eventId}} window={{startTime}}..{{endTime}}"}

_note: One alert per declared transition pair (ADR obs-2 clause 1). It OPENS on
the degraded half appearing in the sink. The N-past-K re-probes emit no
event at all — that is the announce-on-transition ruling doing the work,
not the alert — so they produce zero notifications by construction.
READ `docs/runbooks/alerts.md` § 'What closes it' before believing the
close is caused by the recovery event: it is not, and the message text
below says so rather than lying to the responder.

saved_search.name: {prefix} — degraded ({degraded})
saved_search.select: Timestamp, JSONExtractString(Body, 'event') AS event, JSONExtractString(Body, 'tenant_id') AS tenant_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'connection_id') AS connection_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'correlation_id') AS correlation_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'count') AS count, TraceId AS trace_id
_select_note: The 'one link' fields, and nothing else. core/observability.py ships
structlog's JSONRenderer output as the OTel log record BODY, so every
structured key is inside one JSON string in ClickHouse's `Body` column
and JSONExtractString is how you read it. These columns are what the
alert body carries to the destination (checkAlerts renders up to 5
matching rows as CSV using exactly this select), which is what lets a
responder answer 'what happened' from the message alone.

_threshold_note: EVERY window breach — including the empty ones — and the alert sits in
ALERT for ever with a count of 0. That is not a hypothetical — it is
what an apply with a 0 threshold does, and the dummy receiver is how
1 means 'at least one matching line', which is what a transition alert
wants, and an empty window (0 >= 1 is false) resolves it.
alert.name: {prefix} degraded
alert.message: :rotating_light: OPENED — {prefix} degraded — {degraded} is in the sink. The circuit is DEGRADED. It stays degraded until {recovered} appears in the sink; a 'window quiet' notification from this alert means the 5-minute query window stopped matching, NOT that the circuit recovered. Search the sink for {recovered} before standing down. Runbook: docs/runbooks/alerts.md

_note: THE SECOND HALF OF A TRANSITION PAIR, AND IT IS ITS OWN ALERT.
ADR obs-2 as amended: 'the recovery event is its own
notification ... delivered as a second alert rather than a close'.
WHY IT HAD TO BE A SECOND ALERT. ClickStack's alerting is windowed: an
alert opens when its query window matches and auto-resolves the first
window that does not. So the degraded alert's OK notification means
'the 5-minute window stopped matching', NOT 'the circuit recovered' —
it says so in its own message text, and it fires whether or not the
recovery ever happened. The consequence, confirmed over the wire:
`comms.suppression.recovered` reaches the sink and fires NOTHING unless
something is watching that name.
WHAT IT COSTS, STATED: four notifications per episode instead of two —
degraded OPENS, degraded window-quiets, recovered OPENS, recovered
window-quiets. That is option 2 of the three priced in
docs/runbooks/alerts.md, and it is now the one that is built.
The population is unchanged: this is instantiated from the SAME census
row as `transition`, so a pair still declares two names in one
`events.py` and nobody edits a list.

saved_search.name: {prefix} — recovered ({recovered})
saved_search.select: Timestamp, JSONExtractString(Body, 'event') AS event, JSONExtractString(Body, 'tenant_id') AS tenant_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'connection_id') AS connection_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'correlation_id') AS correlation_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'count') AS count, TraceId AS trace_id
_select_note: The same columns as the degraded half, deliberately: a responder who
read the OPEN should be able to read the all-clear without learning a
second set of fields, and the correlation id is what ties the two

alert.name: {prefix} recovered
alert.message: :white_check_mark: RECOVERED — {prefix} recovered — {recovered} is in the sink. THE CIRCUIT HAS RECOVERED, and this notification is the announcement rather than a close. The degraded alert ({prefix} degraded) does NOT close on this event; its own 'window quiet' means only that its query window stopped matching. This one fires because {recovered} is in the sink, which is the fact you were waiting for. Match it to the OPEN by correlation_id. Runbook: docs/runbooks/alerts.md

_note: One alert per declared spike (census.py's third half). A spike is a
COUNT of one LOG key inside one window, declared in the emitting app's
events.py as SPIKES — key, threshold, window, reason — and never typed
here: this is the shape, the census is the population. The worked
instance is apps/accounts/events.py's auth-failure spike. `interval` is
the declared window and `threshold` the declared count, both filled
from the census row by apply.py; `above` is ClickStack's `>=`, so the
alert opens on the window holding threshold-or-more lines and resolves
on the first window holding fewer. It counts lines, not tenants: the
saved search groups nothing.

saved_search.name: {log_key} — spike
saved_search.select: Timestamp, JSONExtractString(Body, 'event') AS event, JSONExtractString(Body, 'reason') AS reason, JSONExtractString(Body, 'tenant_id') AS tenant_id, JSONExtractString(Body, 'correlation_id') AS correlation_id, TraceId AS trace_id
_name_note: The name carries the key and nothing that can be re-declared: it is
the identity apply.py and export.py match on, so a threshold in it
would turn a re-tuned spike into a second saved search.

alert.name: {log_key} spike
alert.message: :rotating_light: OPENED — {log_key} spike — {threshold} or more {log_key} log lines inside {window} (ClickStack's 'above' is >=). Declared in {declared_at}: {reason}. The rows below say which reason and which tenant; one tenant and twenty tenants are the same alert. A 'window quiet' notification means a {window} window held fewer than {threshold}. Runbook: docs/runbooks/alerts.md § 'Values, and why each one'

_note: The deployment-wide trace alerts (census.py's TRACES), over the Traces
source's server spans. A saved-search alert can only count rows, so this
kind is a DASHBOARD TILE alert: ClickStack's check runs the tile's own
select, which is what lets `latency` carry quantile(0.95). apply.py keeps
one dashboard, one tile per member keyed on the member's key, the alert
embedded in the tile. `above` is ClickStack's >=.

alert.name: {name}
alert.message: :rotating_light: OPENED — {name} — {summary}. A 'window quiet' notification means a {window} window fell back under the threshold. Runbook: docs/runbooks/alerts.md § 'Values, and why each one'

_note: The hard-dependency half (ADR obs-2 clause 2). Outages are /readyz's,
never events — the ruling's scope boundary, held in code. The prober
(prober.sh, the `readyz-prober` service in deploy/compose.yaml) curls
the PUBLIC url every
PROBE_INTERVAL_SECONDS so DNS, TLS and Caddy are in the tested path, and
writes `probe.readyz.failed` / `probe.readyz.ok` into the sink in the
same one-JSON-string shape the app's own log lines have.

saved_search.name: readyz — failing ({failed_event})
saved_search.select: Timestamp, JSONExtractString(Body, 'event') AS event, JSONExtractString(Body, 'target') AS target, JSONExtractString(Body, 'code') AS http_code, JSONExtractString(Body, 'detail') AS detail

alert.name: readyz outage
alert.message: :rotating_light: OPENED — readyz outage — the public /readyz is failing. ClickStack's 'above' is >=, so this fires at 3 or more probe failures inside one minute — at a 15-second probe that is 3 consecutive failures, and one blip never pages. Declared detection window: 3 x 15s = 45s of failing probes, plus up to 60s of ClickStack check latency = under 2 minutes. This alert cannot see the death of the box it runs on — see docs/runbooks/alerts.md § 'What this cannot see'.
